title: English Vocabulary 1 · Units 37–38
description: Unit 37 reviews natural disasters, social and environmental problems, war, strikes and road problems. Unit 38 focuses on everyday have collocations, have got, obligation and common learner errors. Every item has an original example, British English IPA and Portuguese translation in pt only.
sourceNotice: Learning targets are organised from the book’s teaching pages, photographs, examples, learning tips and exercises. All learner examples and editorial notes are newly written; illustrations and source exercises are not reproduced. Exercise-derived and pedagogically extended targets are distinguished using contentOrigin.

units.title: Unit 37 — Global problems
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 37. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.

items.pt: problema global; problema de alcance mundial
items.example: Climate change is a global problem.
items.note: A broad problem that affects many people or places. This phrase adapts the plural wording of the unit title.

items.example: A natural disaster damaged many homes in the region.
items.note: A natural event such as an earthquake, flood or severe storm that causes great damage. This is the theme of Section A.

items.example: A hurricane damaged several houses near the coast.
items.note: A hurricane is a severe tropical storm with extremely strong winds. Do not use this word for every windy day.

items.example: A snowstorm closed the roads to the village.
items.note: A storm with heavy snow and wind. Snowfall refers to snow falling, not necessarily a storm.

items.example: Firefighters tried to stop the forest fire.
items.note: A fire spreading through woodland. Forest fire is a natural noun combination in the source.

items.example: The dry grass can catch fire very quickly.
items.note: Catch fire means begin to burn. The verb catch is irregular: catch, caught, caught.

items.example: There was an earthquake near the city last night.
items.note: An event when the ground shakes because of movement in the Earth. The regular plural is earthquakes.

items.example: The flood destroyed the bridge.
items.note: Flood is a countable noun in this sense: a flood, several floods. Compare the verb flood.

items.example: The town suffered a serious flood in the spring.
items.note: Serious describes how severe the flood is. The source uses the plural form serious floods.

items.example: The river sometimes floods after several days of rain.
items.note: A river floods when water rises beyond its banks. Past simple and past participle: flooded.

items.example: Heavy rain made the river rise quickly.
items.note: Use heavy rain for intense rainfall, not strong rain. Rain is usually uncountable in this context.

items.example: The water reached the top of the river bank.
items.note: A river bank is the land at the side of a river. The source uses river banks in the plural.

items.pt: problema causado por pessoas; problema de origem humana
items.example: Traffic jams are a man-made problem in many cities.
items.note: Man-made means caused or created by human activity. The heading groups several social problems together.

items.example: There are too many people on this bus.
items.note: Use too many before a plural countable noun. Compare too much water or too much pollution with uncountable nouns.

items.example: The city centre was crowded on Saturday.
items.note: A crowded place has too many people in it. The adjective describes places, not a person’s income or housing situation.

items.example: Many crowded cities have traffic problems.
items.note: Crowded cities is reinforced in exercise 37.2. The noun changes to cities in the plural.

items.example: The family was poor but had a safe home.
items.note: Here poor means not having enough money. Someone can be poor without being homeless or unemployed.

items.example: The children were hungry after their long journey.
items.note: Hungry normally means needing food. In this unit it also describes people who do not have enough food.

items.example: The charity offers meals to homeless people.
items.note: Homeless is an adjective meaning without a home. Say homeless people; there is no plural form homeleses.

items.pt: pessoas em situação de rua; pessoas sem moradia
items.example: The local charity provides meals for homeless people.
items.note: An adjective + plural noun expression, explicitly practised in exercise 37.2. Avoid assuming why somebody is homeless.

items.example: He was unemployed for several months.
items.note: Someone who is unemployed does not have a job. Use be unemployed, not have unemployed.

items.example: Pollution is a serious problem near the factory.
items.note: Pollution is normally uncountable: a lot of pollution, not many pollutions.

items.example: The water was too polluted to drink.
items.note: Polluted describes air, water or land made harmful or dirty by pollution. It can be an adjective or participle.

items.example: Old vehicles can pollute the air.
items.note: Pollute is the verb related to the nouns pollution and the adjective polluted. Exercise 37.4 uses the verb.

items.example: Air pollution is worse near busy roads.
items.note: Pollution in the air. Exercise 37.5 practises the full collocation air pollution.

items.example: The war ended before my grandparents were born.
items.note: A war is an extended armed conflict. The source uses the American War of Independence to illustrate the meaning.

items.example: My teacher asked us about the Second World War.
items.note: A world war is a war involving many countries. The First World War is mentioned in exercise 37.5.

items.example: The storm lasted for two hours.
items.note: Last for + a period of time means continue for that duration: lasted for eight years. Last is a verb here.

items.example: The bus drivers announced a strike.
items.note: A strike is a collective refusal to work, usually to request changes in pay or working conditions. Also see on strike.

items.example: The teachers are on strike this week.
items.note: Use be on strike, not be in strike: The teachers are on strike.

items.example: The workers decided to go on strike.
items.note: Go on strike means begin a strike. The past form of go is went: went on strike.

items.example: The workers asked for better pay.
items.note: A worker is a person who works. Workers and low wages appear together in exercise 37.5.

items.example: There was a car crash near the bridge.
items.note: A collision involving a car. In Unit 36, crash also refers to a computer stopping unexpectedly.

items.pt: sofrer um acidente de carro; envolver-se em uma colisão
items.example: She had a car crash on her way home.
items.note: Have a car crash means be involved in a car accident. Had a car crash is the past form.

items.example: There was heavy traffic on the road this morning.
items.note: Traffic refers to vehicles travelling on roads. It is normally uncountable: heavy traffic, not many traffics.

items.example: We were late because of a traffic jam.
items.note: A traffic jam is a line or group of vehicles moving very slowly or unable to move.

items.example: Trains can be very crowded during rush hour.
items.note: Rush hour is the busiest commuting period. Both in the rush hour and during rush hour are natural.

items.example: Buses are often full in the rush hour.
items.note: An expression for the time when roads and public transport are especially busy. The source uses in the rush hour.

items.example: The staff complained about their low wages.
items.note: Low wages are small amounts of pay. Exercise 37.5 links low wages to workers going on strike.

learningObjectives: Recognise hurricanes, snowstorms, forest fires, earthquakes and floods; distinguish flood as a noun and a verb.
Describe natural disasters using catch fire, heavy rain, serious floods and river banks.
Describe crowded places and distinguish poor, hungry, homeless and unemployed.
Use pollution, polluted and pollute in appropriate contexts, and distinguish too many with countable plurals from too much with uncountable nouns.
Talk about war and strikes using last for, be on strike and go on strike.
Describe road problems with car crash, traffic jam and rush hour, including expressions from the exercises.

units.title: Unit 38 — Have / had / had
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 38. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.

items.pt: ter; usar have em expressões cotidianas
items.example: I had lunch early yesterday.
items.note: Have is irregular: have, had, had. In common expressions such as have lunch, it does not simply mean possess.

items.example: We have breakfast at half past seven.
items.note: Breakfast is a meal name: have breakfast without a or an in ordinary contexts.

items.example: I usually have lunch with a colleague.
items.note: Say have lunch to describe eating lunch. Ask What do you have for lunch? to ask about food.

items.example: They had dinner at home on Friday.
items.note: Use have dinner for eating the evening meal. The past form is had dinner.

items.example: We can have a meal before the concert.
items.note: Meal is countable, so use a meal for one occasion. Breakfast, lunch and dinner generally do not need an article.

items.pt: dar uma festa; fazer uma festa
items.example: My neighbours had a party last weekend.
items.note: Have a party means organise or hold a party. Have does not mean own in this expression.

items.example: We have a meeting with the manager tomorrow.
items.note: Use a meeting for one planned discussion, such as a work meeting or a meeting with a teacher.

items.example: Shall we have a game after lunch?
items.note: Have a game means play a game. Add of + sport: have a game of football or tennis.

items.example: Shall we have a game of football this afternoon?
items.note: Have a game of + sport describes taking part in a game. The source uses football as the model sport.

items.example: We have an English lesson every Tuesday.
items.note: Have a lesson often means attend or receive a lesson. It does not necessarily mean teach one.

items.pt: ter uma prova; fazer uma prova
items.example: I have an exam next Wednesday.
items.note: Have an exam means an exam is scheduled or needs to be taken. Use an because exam begins with a vowel sound.

items.pt: ter dever de casa para fazer
items.example: I have homework to finish before tomorrow.
items.note: Have homework means have tasks to complete; do homework means work on those tasks. Homework is uncountable.

items.pt: ter uma avaliação; fazer um teste
items.example: The class has a test on Thursday.
items.note: A study-related collocation given in the learning tip. Compare have an exam and have a lesson.

items.example: I have an English class on Tuesday evenings.
items.note: A study-related collocation mentioned in the learning tip. Class can mean a lesson or a group of students.

items.example: Would you like to have a cup of tea?
items.note: Cup is countable; tea usually names the drink as a substance. You can also say have some tea.

items.example: We had a cup of coffee after the meeting.
items.note: Have a cup of coffee names a serving. Have coffee is also a natural shorter expression.

items.example: I always have coffee before work.
items.note: Practised in exercise 38.1. Have coffee can mean drink coffee without specifying the number of cups.

items.example: You look thirsty; have a drink of water.
items.note: A drink can be water, juice, tea or another beverage. It does not necessarily refer to alcohol.

items.example: The children had an ice cream at the beach.
items.note: An ice cream can mean one serving or item. Ice cream is uncountable when referring to the substance generally.

items.example: Would you like to have some cheese with that?
items.note: Cheese is generally uncountable. Use some cheese for an unspecified quantity.

items.example: I have a shower every morning.
items.note: Common British English expression for washing in a shower. Compare have a bath for bathing in a bathtub.

items.example: She had a bath after a long day.
items.note: A bath normally involves washing in a bathtub. British English uses /ɑː/ in bath.

items.pt: dar um mergulho; nadar um pouco
items.example: We had a swim in the hotel pool.
items.note: Have a swim means spend some time swimming. Swim can also be used as a verb.

items.example: Can I have a look at your new camera?
items.note: Use have a look at + person or thing: Can I have a look at your camera?

items.example: Can I have a go on your bicycle?
items.note: Have a go means try an activity or take a turn. In the source, the speaker asks to try a bicycle.

items.example: Have a good journey! Send me a message when you arrive.
items.note: A polite farewell wish for somebody who is about to travel. Journey refers to the trip.

items.pt: ter um momento; ter um tempinho
items.example: Do you have a moment to talk?
items.note: Do you have a moment? politely asks whether someone has a little time. The article a is important.

items.example: Can I have a word with you after class?
items.note: Have a word with someone means speak to them, usually briefly or privately. A word is singular in this idiom.

items.example: We had a good time at the picnic.
items.note: Have a good time means enjoy an event or activity. Do not confuse it with have time, meaning be available.

items.example: I am going to have my hair cut tomorrow.
items.note: Causative pattern: have + object + past participle. It usually means arrange for another person to cut your hair.

items.example: She is at the hairdresser’s this afternoon.
items.note: The apostrophe indicates the hairdresser’s shop or salon. It is a common British English shortened place name.

items.example: Do you have time to help me?
items.note: Have time means be free or have enough time. Time is uncountable in this use: not have the times.

items.example: I do not have the time to finish the report today.
items.note: Both not have time and not have the time are correct. Do not add a plural -s to time here.

items.example: What do you usually have for lunch?
items.note: The words between have and for lunch are a food or drink: What did you have for lunch?

items.example: I have got two sisters and a brother.
items.note: Have got commonly describes present possession or states, especially in spoken British English. It is not a general past tense.

items.example: I’ve got a spare pen in my bag.
items.note: I’ve is short for I have. I’ve got means I have when describing present possession or a present condition.

items.example: Have you got a map of the city?
items.note: Use Have you got a pen? to ask about possession. Do you have a pen? is also correct.

items.example: Their house has got a large kitchen.
items.note: It’s got means it has got, with it’s as a contraction. Its without an apostrophe is possessive.

items.example: We’ve got ten minutes before the lesson starts.
items.note: We’ve got can refer to available time as well as possessions: We’ve got ten minutes.

items.pt: não ter nenhum(a); não ter nada disponível
items.example: Sorry, we haven’t got any tickets left.
items.note: Use haven’t got any for a present negative. Do not combine do not with have got in this construction.

items.pt: estar com um problema; ter um problema
items.example: I’ve got a problem with my computer.
items.note: A natural spoken expression for a current difficulty. I have a problem is also correct.

items.example: He has got a cold, so he is staying at home.
items.note: Have got a cold and have a cold both describe an illness. Keep a before cold.

items.example: I’ve got a headache after that long meeting.
items.note: Have got a headache describes a current symptom. Headache is countable here: a headache.

items.example: I have a cold and need to rest.
items.note: A pedagogical equivalent of have got a cold. In the past, say had a cold.

items.example: She had a headache yesterday afternoon.
items.note: A pedagogical equivalent of have got a headache. The past form is had a headache.

items.pt: ter de; precisar fazer algo por obrigação
items.section: D · Have got to / Have to
items.example: I have to finish this task before five.
items.note: Have to + base form expresses a requirement or obligation: have to pay. Do not add a second to.

items.pt: ter de; precisar (expressão informal de obrigação)
items.section: D · Have got to / Have to
items.example: I’ve got to leave before the shop closes.
items.note: Have got to expresses obligation, usually in spoken English. It differs from have got for possession.

items.section: D · Have got to / Have to
items.example: Visitors have to pay to enter the museum.
items.note: The source uses admission to a museum to explain have to pay. The base verb follows have to.

items.section: D · Have got to / Have to
items.example: All students have to do an exam at the end of the course.
items.note: Have to do an exam expresses obligation. Contrast have an exam, which refers to an exam being scheduled.

items.pt: ter de ir andando; precisar caminhar
items.section: D · Have got to / Have to
items.example: I’ve got to walk because my car is being repaired.
items.note: A contextual example of necessary action: the speaker needs to walk because the car is unavailable.

items.pt: tive de; teve de; tinha de (obrigação no passado)
items.section: D · Have got to / Have to
items.example: I had to work late yesterday.
items.note: Had to is the usual past form for obligation. The source warns against had got to in this use; note that had got can occur with other meanings.

items.section: D · Have got to / Have to
items.example: Do you have to go to lessons every day?
items.note: Practised in exercise 38.5. Do you have to go to lessons? asks whether attendance is required.

learningObjectives: Use the irregular verb have, had, had with expressions for meals, drinks, recreation, study and washing.
Distinguish have homework from do homework, and have an exam from have to do an exam.
Use have a look at, have a go, have a moment, have a word with and have a good time naturally.
Use the causative phrase have your hair cut and recognise why have cut your hair expresses a different structure.
Use have got for present possession and conditions, including questions, contractions and negative forms.
Distinguish have got for possession from have to and have got to for obligation.
Use had to for past obligation and avoid common errors with articles and plural time expressions.
